book_understanding.teaching_order: A textbook defines factor cost (sum of factor incomes), defines market price as factor cost plus net indirect taxes, and then gives an example. Here the example comes first and breaks twice: the previous video's laptop sale gives GDP 15,000; the narrator points out that tax was ignored, adds 20% at each step and gets 18,000; 'so is GDP 15,000 or 18,000?' forces the two terms, which arrive as names for two numbers the learner already holds. Only then is factor cost built from a factory's bills and market price written as a formula, and a 3-year what-if shows why the choice matters. The order works because each term answers a contradiction the learner has just seen.
book_understanding.breakdown_rule: Each new piece is forced by a gap in the previous example (no tax, then two answers, then what each answer is made of, then what happens over time), and every piece reuses the same laptop numbers.

talmel_summary: In the number parts the fit is tight: each actor and number lands on its spoken word (shopkeeper, 10,000, 15,000, +5,000, tax, 15K or 18K), and the two GDP branches first carry the two numbers and are then renamed with the two terms as they are said. The factory part shows the step as a table that fills with its amounts; terms there tend to appear about 1 s before they are said. Weak points: a 12 s transcript gap at 14.7-26.9 s, a label that says 'price' where the speech says cost, 'Year 2020' and the 20% rate never said or never shown, and a green highlight that jumps to Market Price while the voice still describes the old factor cost practice.

voice.notes: About 186 words per minute, quick and friendly, teacher-to-student ('dekhiye', 'kya aapne notice kiya', 'maan ke chalte hain'). Numbers are read in full ('das hazaar', 'pandrah hazaar', '1 lakh') and every result is restated with 'to iska matlab yah hua ki'. The learner is addressed as 'you as an entrepreneur', which turns the factor list into the listener's own bills. Ends on an open question rather than a summary.

game_ideas.player_does: Moves one laptop from the factory to the shop to the customer; at each arrow the government sets a tax rate and maybe a subsidy, and the player must add the right amount to the price tag before passing it on.
game_ideas.process_happens: TAX badges drop on the arrows, the price tag grows (10K, +2K, +5K, +1K = 18K), and two meters at the India map fill separately: factor cost (10K + 5K) and market price (18K). A subsidy chip lowers only the market price meter.
game_ideas.win: Both meters correct: GDP at factor cost 15,000, at market price 18,000 (or the subsidy-adjusted value).
game_ideas.lose: Putting tax into the factor cost meter makes it flash and shows a factory worker asking 'who earned this 2,000?' (nobody: it went to the government).
game_ideas.concept: market price = factor cost + indirect taxes - subsidies

game_ideas.player_does: Runs the laptop factory for a month: pays rent for the land, wages to workers, interest to the bank and sets the owner's profit, then chooses how many laptops to make.
game_ideas.process_happens: Each payment flies to its owner (landlord, workers, bank, entrepreneur) and stacks into a 'factor payments' column; dividing by the laptops made gives the factor cost tag on each laptop.
game_ideas.win: Matches a target factor cost (for example 10K per laptop) with all four factors paid.
game_ideas.lose: Dragging the electricity bill or raw material into the factor column is rejected with 'this was bought from another firm, not paid to a factor' (the game follows the textbook rule, not the video's mixed list).
game_ideas.concept: factors of production and their payments

game_ideas.player_does: Reads three years of headlines claiming 'GDP up!' and must check each against the factory's output and the tax rate.
game_ideas.process_happens: The factory shows the same single laptop each year while the tax slider rises; the market price bar climbs 18K, 20K, 25K and the factor cost bar stays at 15K.
game_ideas.win: Flags every headline that used market price and rewrites it with factor cost ('production flat').
game_ideas.lose: Accepting a headline makes a crowd celebrate while the factory still turns out one laptop; the tax arrow lights up as the real cause.
game_ideas.concept: 3-year what-if: taxes raise GDP at market price, production flat

checks_learned: Every term in a formula (here subsidies) must get a number in the worked example at least once, or the script must say why it is zero.
Every number the narration computes (the shopkeeper's 12,000) should appear on the picture where it belongs.
On-screen labels must use the word being taught: a factor cost result must not be labelled 'price'.
A highlight must not jump to the opposite answer while the voice is still on the old one (Market Price lit while 'factor cost' is being said).
A single transcript word stretched over more than 5 s hides a gap (14.7-26.9 s here) and must be flagged like a missing stretch.
Real brand names on generic icons (a bank) must be replaced with a generic bank.
When the narration lists factor payments, a classification check should flag intermediate inputs (electricity, maintenance, raw material) put in the factor column.
The most exam-relevant point should not be left as a comment-box question; if the answer is deferred, the script must link it.

teaching_best.why: The narrator breaks his own example ('we never counted tax, that is unrealistic'), so the next idea grows out of a visible gap.
'Is GDP 15,000 or 18,000?' makes the learner hold two numbers before the two terms are named; the terms then feel necessary.
Addressing the learner as an entrepreneur paying rent, wages and interest turns factor payments into bills the learner can picture.
The 3-year what-if holds production fixed and moves only taxes, so the reason to prefer factor cost is seen, not asserted.

teaching_weak.why: About 12 s of the answer (the shop's costs) is missing from the transcript, right where the first idea is built.
Capital is shown buying raw material, machines, marketing and transport, which mixes factor payments with input purchases.
The shop's factor cost includes electricity and maintenance, which are intermediate costs; doubtful.
Subsidies are in the formula but never in the numbers.
The reason for India's 2015 switch is left as homework, so the video ends without a recap or the real-world answer.
